Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 422:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (10/10)

My god, Paul Wang has done it again. If [i]Sabres of Infinity[/i] was a baptism by fire, [i]Guns of Infinity [/i]is the aftermath that comes after: the trauma that scars your body, your honor, and your soul. The sequel is grander, darker, and far more morally tangled, and your officer becomes a legend or a ghost buried under the weight of their own decisions. 

💂‍♂️ [b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*]Narrative ambition. Guns is an exceptional piece of serialized storytelling, continuing your personal saga seamlessly from Sabres. It not only recalls ALL your choices but builds entire arcs around them. Your reputation, your leadership style, your allies, your enemies—every thread you spun in the previous game returns to either lift you up or tear you down. Few interactive novels feel this alive to your past actions. And of course, this game only builds on all that. No longer are you a mere soldier; you can rise to the rank of Major (I did!) and command multiple squads.

[*] Even more branching! Now there’s Chapter 2A or 2B. Offhand remarks, political leanings, decisions made under pressure are all small details that accumulate and continue to register all the way to the finale. The inclusion of the secret “disgraced” path is especially impressive; instead of cutting you off for failing, the game offers an entirely different narrative that feels intentional rather than punitive. It’s one of the few IF titles where failure opens doors instead of slamming them.

[*]Writing style. Wang’s prose remains some of the best in all of Hosted Games. The tone is disciplined and militaristic, yet surprisingly lyrical, creating a vivid sense of time and place without excess ornamentation. Battle scenes feel chaotic but readable; quiet moments carry emotional weight without melodrama. The scene of the men singing before combat is a perfect example! It’s simple and restrained, yet so human in the need for connection before battle. The writing understands the emotional contradictions of command: the strategic calculus, the private grief, and the way duty hollows a person out one decision at a time.

[*] Maturity and moral weight. Sabres was rather lighthearted, but Guns goes all the way into the necessity, or lack thereof, of war. He tackles my favorite question: “honor or duty?” I don’t want to spoil anything, but your morals will be tested again and again, in the face of riches, fame, or the woman you love. You’ll have to commit to a path at the end of the book, and I was so stressed I had to look up what everyone was saying on Reddit because I wanted to make the right choice!!! But there are no right choices, only the one you can live with.

[*]UI. There's more subtleties to the UI: better pictures, chapter headings, etc. The glossary and lore continue to shine, and the consistent worldbuilding is just [i]chef’s kiss.[/i]

[*] THERE IS NOW ROMANCE. You’ll have two captivating female romance options. But of course in typical Wang fashion, even romance doesn’t come easily. Relationships require timing, restraint, and sacrifice, and they complicate your loyalties rather than softening the story. Still, it’s beautifully written. [spoiler]Mfw when I choose to commit warcrimes for the woman I love.[/spoiler]

[*]Family is now added! You can choose your relationship with your father and mother and younger siblings, if you have any. There’s also a new gameplay mechanic added—debt—which will come into play in the later books. Both are fantastic additions, giving the serious universe a much needed emotional angle.

[*] Length. One playthrough took me 6 hours, though I am a fast reader. Nothing—not even the climax—felt rushed at all.
[/list]

[b]⚰️ Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*]Steeper difficulty. This entry is harder, both narratively and mechanically. Fail a few stat checks and you can find yourself buried under the weight of bad rolls or poor planning. Many times, I was only 2 or 3 percent away from passing a check and was forced to take a suboptimal outcome. It’s tough because your build depends on your earlier save, but you might not have known to focus on 1-2 skills, or which choice gives the “best” option.

[*]Still narrow in scope. As before, you’re a male officer in a very specific setting. That limited perspective keeps the story focused, but also cuts off room for roleplay diversity. 
[/list]

Verbose, light on choices, punishing and unclear. That's how I'd describe both Guns and Sabres of Infinity. In both you're constantly reading through half a dozen densely packed screens of paragraphs with no input, sometimes only offered a 'choice' of your opinion (meaningless) before being treated to another deluge of indulgent descriptions lasting another 6+ screens. 

It's also so very punishing, and trying to manage all the various meters that dictate your effectiveness in skill checks is exhausting--and unclear. Choices are grayed-out and unavailable with no explanation, choices are presented without any ability to anticipate their outcome, hours of meager progress in a particular skill/attribute is undone by a single decision whose outcome you couldn't have predicted. It's a frustrating, mostly infuriating experience that has me disgusted after wasting so many hours in. 

Finally, there are scenarios that cannot be overcome, representing 'hard stops' that for whatever reason (be it the compilation of previous decisions or individual characteristics of how your character is built) are 100% failure or at the very least a presentation of only bad outcomes. 

I wouldn't recommend this punishing, joyless slog to my worst enemy.

This review will cover both Sabers and Guns of Infinity (hereafter "Infinity"), as the games go together.

I enjoyed the games. Author Paul Wang has an obvious talent for writing and a passion for military and political history, and this imbues his work with considerable verisimilitude. Wang gives you a canvas on which to write your own heroes, and you can play everything from a gallant, idealistic knight to a learned, tactical genius to a savage, selfish blackguard. Infinity's secondary characters are also complex and memorable; none more so than the bastard-born, fatalistic, ruthless Cazarosta. 

The replay value is excellent, indeed you get to experience completely new scenes and battles in each run. There are some Choice Games that would have been better as novels...but Infinity is not among them, it embraces its art form with gusto and is the better for it.

That said, the gameplay has some flaws. Infinity has so many hidden stat boosts that it is completely unclear for a new player how to generate a solid character (and the game does not telegraph that you are missing them). On my first playthrough, I had an ostensibly successful run through Sabers as an Idealistic/Merciful Soldiering Build, but later found out that my character was so gimped I was *unable* to clear the Forlorn Hope section in Guns, and had to abandon the run.

It is additionally frustrating to manage the stats of the soldiers under your command. From solely reading the gamebook, I found it wholly opaque how the game decides if it's going to stat-check Discipline or Morale or Loyalty (or Strength), or do multiple checks. I eventually had to look at guides and use repeated trial-and-error to figure it out.

That said, this game has built a passionate fanbase that is willing to help you through the gameplay, so that goes a way in mitigating these issues.

In sum, I recommend purchasing Infinity and giving it a few runs. I found it engaging despite the aforementioned flaws.

Review: This is the best CYOA game to be released by Hosted, bar none. It continues where the first game, Sabres of Infinity, left off, following the rise (or fall) of the protagonist, a dragoon officer. The writing is largely reminiscent of Napoleonic fiction, and I wouldn't be surprised if the author had a stack of Bernard Cornwell's novels at hand for reference in writing the material. That being said, the game world is wholly original and incredibly immersive, and I always enjoy coming back to the richly detailed characters and locales.

Importantly, the gameplay is much improved since the first game, particularly in regards to balancing. Where one found min-maxing inevitable in the previous installment, the choices offered and their influence on the main character in both stats and relationships is far more nuanced and a bit more forgiving in this game. That being said, you can find yourself in no-win scenarios if you plunge your character into deeds of daring far beyond their capabilities, which I enjoy.

If you need a military-fiction fix, or are thinking about trying a CYOA game for the first time, this is your best bet.
